{% extends "base_livecode.html" %} {% block title %}Scheme macros: an interactive Tutorial{% endblock %} {% block content %} In Scheme, we generally define lambda's in the following manner:
(lambda (x) x)
This is the most basic one you can define, with the first x as the binding variable and the second x as the bound one, aka the identity.
Now, we define a procedure f, which normally we do as (define (f x) x), but that's actually sugar for
(define f (lambda (x) x)) f
Here's an identity function lambda that acts as a procedure, the entire block (lambda (x) x) is the procedure taking the input (+ 3 4)
((lambda (x) x) (+ 3 4))
Any let can be defined by lambda in Scheme. In fact, one can define let using a macro, introduced later. let is used to create local variable bindings, such as (+ 3 4) being bound to x
(let ((x (+ 3 4))) x)
Here we see an example of two (as far as Scheme is concerned) identical expressions.
((lambda (y) (* y y)) (+ 3 4))
(let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y))
There's also a ' quote operator, which essentially stops the evaluation of an expression and treats it as just data. This means the code becomes data. Then there's eval, which forces Scheme to evaluate an expression. In a way, eval is a little compiler in the program that you hand a list of symbols and numbers, and it treats it as a line of code.
(eval '(+ 3 4))
eval runs a piece of code. expand stops one step earlier: it takes a piece of code and shows what it looks like after all macros are filled in, without running anything. Notice (+ 3 4) stays (+ 3 4) in the output below, not 7. Expansion is about syntax, not values.

Two things change in the output. First, + and * become #2%+ (or $primitive 2 + depending on if you're in the repl or not) and #2%*. The expander has resolved those names to Chez's built-in primitives, so later stages know nobody redefined them. Second, y is replaced with a generated symbol (a "gensym") like #{y hd68jsbgg52bmdgo8xk3b4q0d-0}. The expander renames every bound variable to a fresh, globally unique name. Note that in Chez the expansion still prints as let; other Schemes rewrite it to lambda, which is the same thing, as shown before!
(expand '(let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y)))
The gensyms are hard and annoying to read. (print-gensym #f) suppresses the uniquely identifying suffix and prints just the original name. Tihe symbols are still unique internally; only the printing changes and allows for ease-of-reading.
(print-gensym #f)
(expand '(let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y)))
That hides a bit too much though: if two different variables both happened to be named y, we'd have no way to tell them apart anymore. So as a middle ground there's (print-gensym 'pretty/suffix), which prints the original name plus a tiny numeric suffix, like y.1.
(print-gensym 'pretty/suffix)
(expand '(let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y)))
If we expand the lambda version from earlier, we get the exact same thing. Essentially, whenever the expander sees a lambda sitting directly in the operator position, it just turns it into a let. So as far as Scheme is concerned the two spellings are one and the same program.
(expand '((lambda (y) (* y y)) (+ 3 4)))
We know what the quote operator does, but clearly it would be a bit of a pain to write the following let, quoting every single symbol one by one.
(let ((adj 'little)) (list 'Mary 'had 'a adj 'lamb))
The easier way to do this is to use the quasiquote `, which essentially quotes everything inside in the same manner as above, except for anything marked with the unquote operator ,, which gets evaluated and dropped in.
(let ((adj 'little)) `(Mary had a ,adj lamb))
Unquote works anywhere inside the quasiquote, including the operator position. Here we're building the list (+ 3 4). Note that nothing actually gets added, it's still just a list of three things, not a computation.
(let ((op '+)) `(,op 3 4))
But since it's just data, we can hand it to eval and it becomes code, so now we get 7. The rest of the tutorial will have more examples where we build up some code as a list with quasiquote and then run it.
(eval (let ((op '+)) `(,op 3 4)))
If we swap what's in the hole, the same template gives us different code. This is essentially the whole idea behind a macro, a template with holes in it which gets filled in and then treated as code rather than passing arguments like a normal function.
(eval (let ((op '*)) `(,op 3 4)))
Here's the same trick, but now the hole is a variable name. We're generating a let that binds whatever name var happens to hold, so running this gives back (let ((x 3)) (* x x)).
(let ((var 'x)) `(let ((,var 3)) (* ,var ,var)))
Now suppose the body also comes from outside, say from whoever is using our template. Their body (x 4) refers to their own x, presumably some procedure. But our template also happened to pick x as its binding name, so what comes out is (let ((x 3)) (x 4)), aka our binding shadows theirs, and since this was unintentional it's called being "captured". If you try wrapping this in eval you get attempt to apply non-procedure 3. This is called variable capture, and it's essentially the problem that hygiene exists to solve.
A macro system is hygienic if it guarantees this specific thing won't happen, this collision essentially of names introduced by the macro and names written by the user of the macro. The word "hygiene" means clean, after all. Macros will be introduced later, but keep this in mind.
(let ((var 'x) (body '(x 4))) `(let ((,var 3)) ,body))
The obvious fix is to just not pick a name the user could have picked. gensym gives us a fresh symbol that's guaranteed to be different from every other symbol in the program (with pretty/suffix on, it prints as x.0). Now the binding is x.0 and the body's x is left alone, still pointing at whatever x meant outside.
(let ((var (gensym "x")) (body '(x 4))) `(let ((,var 3)) ,body))
Every call to gensym hands back a brand new symbol, never one it's handed out before. Here's the same code three times, collected in a list, and the suffix just keeps counting up.
(list (let ((var (gensym "x")) (body '(x 4))) `(let ((,var 3)) ,body)) (let ((var (gensym "x")) (body '(x 4))) `(let ((,var 3)) ,body)) (let ((var (gensym "x")) (body '(x 4))) `(let ((,var 3)) ,body)))
Quick detour on define before we write a real macro. These two are the same thing, the second is just shorthand for the first. Both are procedures, and we call them the usual way. Throwback to the top of the tutorial on the syntactic sugar.
(define my-proc (lambda (x) (* x x))) (my-proc 3)
(define (my-proc x) (* x x)) (my-proc 3)
Now for the real thing... define-syntax with syntax-rules defines a macro, which is essentially a pattern on the left and a template on the right. Whenever the expander sees something matching (my-let ((id e)) body), it replaces it with ((lambda (id) body) e), with id, e, and body filled in from the match. This is exactly the let/lambda equivalence from earlier, just written down as a rewrite rule. Note that unlike the quasiquote version, we never call eval: the expander does the rewriting for us before the program even runs. In fact, that's fundamentally the difference between a macro and a procedure. A procedure receives values at run time, while a macro receives code at expansion time and hands back different code, which is then compiled like anything else. (This block gets loaded into the blocks below.)
(define-syntax my-let (syntax-rules () [(my-let ((id e)) body) ((lambda (id) body) e)]))
And it works just like let.
(my-let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y))
If we expand it, we see that my-let is gone entirely. It became a lambda application, which Chez then prints as a let, identical to what we saw before. The compiler never even knows my-let existed. Notice y got renamed to something like y.1, same as before.
(expand '(my-let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y)))
So where does that renaming actually come from? Detective time! Here the template uses my-lambda, which isn't defined anywhere.
(define-syntax my-let (syntax-rules () [(my-let ((id e)) body) ((my-lambda (id) body) e)]))
expand still goes through, since expanding doesn't run anything. But if you look at the output, y is not renamed this time. The expander only renames variables it knows are bound, and it has no idea my-lambda binds anything, so it treats (my-lambda (y) (* y y)) as an ordinary procedure call with two arguments and y is just a free variable. In other words hygiene comes from the expander understanding which forms bind names, it doesn't just naively go for everything.
(expand '(my-let ((y (+ 3 4))) (* y y)))
let* is essentially let with the bindings done in order, where each one can see the ones before it. Here x is 9, y is 81, then a second y is 9 + 81 = 90, and the result is 9 * 90 = 810.
(let* ((x (+ 4 5)) (y (* x x)) (y (+ x y))) (* x y))
Which is to say, it's really just nested lets. Same answer.
(let ((x (+ 4 5))) (let ((y (* x x))) (let ((y (+ x y))) (* x y))))
expand confirms it. And notice! let* isn't primitive, it's a macro over let. Notice the two ys get different suffixes, since the second one shadows the first, and the renaming makes that visible.
(expand '(let* ((x (+ 4 5)) (y (* x x)) (y (+ x y))) (* x y)))
We can even write it ourselves. There are two rules this time though If there are no bindings left, the result is just the body, otherwise we peel off the first binding into a let and recurse on the rest. The ... in the pattern matches zero or more of whatever comes right before it, and in the template it repeats them. So the macro is recursive, and the expander just keeps expanding until there's no my-let* left.
(define-syntax my-let* (syntax-rules () [(my-let* () body) body] [(my-let* ((id e) (id* e*) ...) body) (let ((id e)) (my-let* ((id* e*) ...) body))]))
Here's the built-in one again, for comparison.
(let* ((x (+ 4 5)) (y (* x x)) (y (+ x y))) (* x y))
And here's ours.
(my-let* ((x (+ 4 5)) (y (* x x)) (y (+ x y))) (* x y))
And the expansion is the same as the built-in's, right down to the shape.
(expand '(my-let* ((x (+ 4 5)) (y (* x x)) (y (+ x y))) (* x y)))
